lead: Humidity sensors measure how much water vapour is in the air. The useful quantity is usually relative humidity at a stated temperature, because the same air shows a different RH after a small temperature change. A sensor turns water uptake or dew formation into a capacitance, a resistance or an optical signal. You meet these devices in air conditioners, grain stores, incubators, ventilators and data centres.
prereq: You need the parallel-plate capacitance from capacitive transducers (C = εA/d, where C is capacitance, ε is permittivity, A is electrode area and d is spacing), thermistors from resistive transducers, and the general sensor chain in chemical sensors and biosensors.

sections.h3: Three ways to describe water vapour

blocks.text: Absolute humidity is the mass of water vapour in one cubic metre of air, in grams per cubic metre (g/m³). It stays the same on heating or cooling only if the volume is fixed, as in a sealed box. Open air expands when heated, so its g/m³ falls a little; the mass of water per kilogram of dry air (the mixing ratio) and the dew point stay fixed.
Relative humidity (RH) is the actual water vapour pressure divided by the saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature, times 100:

blocks.where: p<sub>v</sub> is the actual partial pressure of water vapour in pascals (Pa); p<sub>sat</sub>(T) is the saturation vapour pressure at temperature T in kelvin (K); RH is in percent. Warm air holds more vapour, so p<sub>sat</sub>(T) rises with T; the same p<sub>v</sub> gives a lower RH after heating.

blocks.text: Dew point is the temperature at which p<sub>sat</sub> equals p<sub>v</sub>. At dew point, RH is 100 %. A surface colder than the dew point collects condensation. Dew point is an absolute measure: warming the air does not change it unless water is added or removed.

These three numbers answer different questions. Absolute humidity gives the amount of water; RH gives how close the air is to condensation at the current temperature; dew point gives the temperature at which condensation starts. A humidity sensor usually reports RH, so it must also state the temperature of measurement.

In hospitals humidity is a treatment variable, not only a comfort figure. A neonatal incubator holds a set RH so that a premature baby does not lose water through its thin skin. A ventilator's heated humidifier delivers gas near 100 % RH at about 37 °C, which is about 44 mg of water per litre, because dry gas damages the airway. Operating theatres keep RH within a set band, typically about 40 to 60 %, to limit static sparks and microbial growth. Each of these loops uses a capacitive sensor read together with a temperature sensor.

A capacitive humidity sensor uses a thin hygroscopic polymer film, such as polyimide, between two electrodes. Dry polymer has a dielectric constant near 3. Water has a dielectric constant near 80. As the polymer absorbs water vapour, its effective dielectric constant rises, so capacitance rises:

blocks.where: C is capacitance in farads (F); ε<sub>r</sub> is the relative permittivity (dielectric constant); ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.854 × 10<sup>−12</sup> F/m; A is electrode area in square metres; d is film thickness in metres. The film is thin, so C is small; cable and stray capacitance can matter. A guard ring or a reference capacitor helps.

blocks.text: A resistive humidity sensor uses a porous ceramic such as Al2O3 or TiO2. Water adsorbed on the pore walls forms ions, so surface conduction increases and resistance falls, often by orders of magnitude from dry to wet. The curve is less linear than the capacitive type. The ceramic may need periodic heating to clean the surface. The same surface-adsorption idea drives gas-sensitive resistors.

Both types use AC excitation, typically about 1 kHz. DC would polarise the polymer and electrolyse the water film, causing drift and damage. The AC signal must be small. Datasheets quote response time to a step, hysteresis between rising and falling RH, and temperature coefficient in %RH per °C. A thermal conductivity sensor uses two thermistors: one sealed dry and one exposed. Water vapour changes the thermal conductivity and heat capacity of air, so the exposed thermistor cools differently; the resistance difference gives humidity. It is less selective but works in hot, dirty air.

Saturated salt solutions give a known RH in a sealed jar at a fixed temperature. Common points are LiCl at about 11 % RH, MgCl<sub>2</sub> at about 33 % RH and NaCl at about 75 % RH. Place the sensor in the headspace above the slurry, wait for equilibrium, and record the reading. Two or three points give offset and slope. A capacitive sensor is close to straight between 20 % and 80 % RH; do not assume it stays straight near 95 % RH, where saturation bends the curve.

A chilled mirror hygrometer is an accurate reference. It cools a small mirror until dew forms. A light source and photodetector watch the reflected light; dew scatters it. A control loop holds the mirror at the dew-point temperature, read by a thermometer. The method is direct and accurate but slow, costly and sensitive to dirt on the mirror.

A practical reading is complete only with its temperature, calibration history and uncertainty. Quote response time, hysteresis and temperature coefficient in the specification. In a grain store or a server room, a slow sensor can miss a fast change, and a sensor near a cold wall can read a different RH from the room air. Mount it where air moves and where condensation cannot form on the active surface.

figure.caption: Left: the sensor reads 100 pF at 20 % RH and 160 pF at 80 % RH, so 145 pF means 65 % RH. Right: the same 1.90 kPa of vapour is 60.0 % RH at 25 °C but 33.8 % at 35 °C, because the saturation curve rises; the line meets the curve at the dew point, 16.7 °C.

examples.question: A capacitive humidity sensor is linear. It reads 100 pF at 20 % RH and 160 pF at 80 % RH. A room reads 145 pF. Find the RH. Also state the sensitivity and the zero-RH intercept.
steps: Write the straight-line relation C = m·RH + b, where C is capacitance in pF, RH is in percent, m is the slope in pF per %RH, and b is the intercept in pF.
Intercept b = C1 − m·RH1 = 100 − 1 × 20 = 80 pF. This is the extrapolated value at 0 % RH, not a measured point.
The sensitivity is 1 pF per %RH, the intercept is 80 pF, and the room RH is 65 %.
examples.answer: The room is at 65 % RH, with sensitivity 1 pF/%RH and zero-RH intercept 80 pF.
examples.check:
C1 = 100.0
RH1 = 20.0
C2 = 160.0
RH2 = 80.0
Croom = 145.0
m = (C2 - C1) / (RH2 - RH1)
b = C1 - m * RH1
RH = (Croom - b) / m
print(m)
print(b)
print(RH)

examples.question: Room air at 25 °C has a water vapour pressure of 1.90 kPa. The saturation vapour pressure is 3.169 kPa at 25 °C and 5.627 kPa at 35 °C; the Magnus formula p<sub>sat</sub> = 0.6109 exp(17.625 T / (T + 243.04)) kPa, with T in °C, gives it at other temperatures. (a) Find the RH. (b) The air is warmed to 35 °C in an incubator with no water added. Find the new RH. (c) Find the dew point.
steps: (b) Warming adds no water, so p<sub>v</sub> stays 1.90 kPa while p<sub>sat</sub> rises: RH = 100 × 1.90 / 5.627 = 33.8 %.
(c) At the dew point p<sub>sat</sub>(T) = p<sub>v</sub>. Invert the Magnus formula: ln(1.90 / 0.6109) = 1.1346, so T = 243.04 × 1.1346 / (17.625 − 1.1346) = 275.75 / 16.490 = 16.7 °C.
Check: the dew point is the same 16.7 °C in (a) and (b), because the amount of vapour did not change. A window colder than 16.7 °C would collect dew.
examples.answer: The RH is 60.0 % at 25 °C and 33.8 % after warming to 35 °C; the dew point stays at about 16.7 °C.
examples.check:
import math
pv = 1.90
print(round(100 * pv / 3.169, 1))
print(round(100 * pv / 5.627, 1))
g = math.log(pv / 0.6109)
print(round(243.04 * g / (17.625 - g), 1))

traps: Using a DC ohmmeter on a resistive humidity sensor. DC electrolyses the water film, polarises the ceramic and makes the resistance drift; use the specified AC excitation.
Reporting RH without the temperature. Heating the same air lowers RH even though the amount of water and the dew point are unchanged.
Extrapolating the straight 20–80 % calibration line to 95 % RH. Polymer sensors bend near saturation, and the error can be several %RH.
Ignoring cable capacitance on a capacitive sensor. A few tens of pF of cable can look like a large RH error; keep leads short and use the guard or reference.

quiz.q: Define relative humidity and write its formula.
quiz.a: RH = 100 × p<sub>v</sub> / p<sub>sat</sub>(T), where p<sub>v</sub> is actual vapour pressure and p<sub>sat</sub>(T) is saturation vapour pressure at temperature T; RH is in percent.

quiz.q: Why are capacitive and resistive humidity sensors excited with AC rather than DC?
quiz.a: AC avoids polarisation of the polymer and electrolysis of the water film. DC causes drift and damage; about 1 kHz is common.

quiz.q: A linear capacitive humidity sensor reads 90 pF at 30 % RH and 150 pF at 70 % RH. Find the RH when it reads 120 pF.
A sensor near a cold wall reads 75 % RH while the room air reads 60 % RH. The absolute humidity is the same. Explain.
quiz.a: The wall cools nearby air. Saturation vapour pressure falls with temperature, so the same actual vapour pressure gives a higher RH. The wall reading is local; moving air gives room RH.

quiz.q: At about 75 % RH, a NaCl salt jar is the reference. The sensor reads 72 % RH. Find the offset and the corrected reading.
quiz.a: Offset = measured − reference = 72 − 75 = −3 %RH. Corrected reading = measured + 3 = 75 %RH.

quiz.q: Why is a chilled mirror hygrometer accurate but slow?
quiz.a: It measures dew point directly, so it does not depend on a polymer calibration. The mirror must cool, dew must form and the optical loop must settle, so response is slow; dirt on the mirror also affects it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Product humidity sensors join a polymer capacitor, a band-gap temperature sensor and a digital interface, so the output is already linearised and temperature-compensated; that is a smart sensor, see smart sensors. Search “polyimide capacitive humidity sensor”, “chilled mirror hygrometer” and “saturated salt calibration”.
